title: India Just Scrapped Capital Gains Tax on Foreign Bond Investments. Here Is Why NRIs Should Care.
excerpt: The cabinet approved eliminating the 12.5 per cent tax on government securities as the rupee slides and oil threatens inflation. The RBI decides on rates tomorrow.
body:
India's cabinet has approved a plan to scrap capital gains tax on foreign portfolio investments in government securities, a move designed to attract overseas capital into Indian debt at a moment when the rupee is under sustained pressure and oil prices are threatening to reignite inflation.

The decision, first reported by The Economic Times and confirmed by a source familiar with the matter to Reuters, would eliminate the 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains tax that foreign investors currently pay on listed government bonds held longer than 12 months. A separate 20 per cent withholding tax on interest income may also be removed, the source said.

The timing is not subtle. The Indian rupee has weakened more than 5 per cent since January, squeezed by elevated crude oil prices near $97 a barrel and a net $28 billion in foreign portfolio outflows from Indian equities this year. While foreign investors have maintained positive inflows into Indian government debt — investing a net $1.4 billion — policymakers clearly want to accelerate that trend.

## What It Means in Practice

Under current rules, a foreign investor who buys Indian government bonds and sells them at a profit after 12 months pays 12.5 per cent on the gain. That tax, combined with the 20 per cent withholding on coupon payments, has long made Indian sovereign debt less competitive than bonds from peer emerging markets that offer more favourable tax treatment.

Removing both levies would put India roughly in line with global standards. Most major bond markets — including the United States, United Kingdom, and much of the European Union — do not impose capital gains taxes on non-resident holdings of government debt. India has been an outlier, and that gap has cost it capital.

The benchmark 10-year Indian government bond yield eased one basis point to 7.01 per cent on Thursday, a modest initial reaction. The real impact will depend on when the policy takes effect and whether it is accompanied by broader reforms to settlement infrastructure and access rules that foreign institutional investors have long cited as friction points.

## The RBI Meeting Looms Large

The tax decision lands one day before the Reserve Bank of India announces its monetary policy decision on Friday — widely expected to be one of the most closely watched in recent memory. Nearly 80 per cent of economists in a Reuters poll expect the central bank to hold its repo rate at 5.25 per cent, but overnight indexed swaps are already pricing in a rate hike, reflecting market anxiety about inflation.

The Beige Book-style data from the Fed in the United States paints a similar picture on the other side of the world. Rising energy costs from the Iran conflict are filtering through to shipping, groceries, and fertiliser prices, creating what analysts describe as a stagflationary combination of weakening consumer demand and rising cost pressures.

For the RBI, the calculus is delicate. Hiking rates would support the rupee and signal inflation-fighting resolve, but it would also raise borrowing costs for an economy still digesting the impact of $97 oil. Holding steady risks further currency weakness if the Fed under new Chair Kevin Warsh moves toward tightening at his debut FOMC meeting on June 17.

## What NRI Investors Should Consider

For the Indian diaspora holding investments across both markets, the developments create a rare alignment of opportunity and risk.

On the opportunity side, Indian government bonds yielding 7 per cent with no capital gains tax and potentially no withholding tax would be among the most attractive sovereign debt plays in the emerging-market universe. NRIs who have avoided Indian fixed income because of tax drag and repatriation friction may find the proposition materially different if the reforms are implemented cleanly.

On the risk side, the rupee's slide means that dollar-denominated returns on Indian assets are being eroded even as nominal yields remain high. An NRI earning 7 per cent in rupee terms but losing 5 per cent to currency depreciation is effectively earning 2 per cent before adjusting for any remaining transaction costs. The RBI's Friday decision — and its tone on inflation and currency defence — will shape whether that calculus improves or worsens.

The broader context is a government that appears willing to make structural concessions to attract foreign capital at a moment of genuine macroeconomic stress. Whether the market rewards that openness depends on execution, timing, and the trajectory of oil prices that remain stubbornly beyond New Delhi's control.
